lessons.title: Java Basics
lessons.description: Section 1 · Programming Fundamentals. Explain how the JDK, JRE and JVM work together to compile and run Java.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Explain how the JDK, JRE and JVM work together to compile and run Java.
- Use variables, primitive types, operators, input/output and command-line arguments.
- Write methods and work with arrays, strings and wrapper classes.

## Introduction to Java
Java is a general-purpose, statically typed, object-oriented language. You write source code in `.java` files, the compiler turns it into **bytecode** (`.class` files), and the Java Virtual Machine runs that bytecode on any operating system that has a JVM. This "write once, run anywhere" model is why Java powers backend services, Android apps, banking systems and big-data tools.

Key characteristics you will rely on throughout this course:
- **Statically typed:** every variable has a declared type that the compiler checks before the program runs.
- **Object-oriented:** programs are built from classes and objects (Module 2).
- **Garbage collected:** the JVM frees memory that is no longer reachable, so you do not call `free` yourself.
- **Huge standard library:** collections, I/O, networking, concurrency and date/time come built in.

## Setting up: JDK, IDE and the JVM
### Install the JDK
Download a current LTS JDK (Java 21 is a good choice) from a vendor such as Oracle, Eclipse Temurin or Microsoft. After installing, open a new terminal and check both tools:

```bash
java --version
javac --version
```

If `javac` is "not recognized", the JDK `bin` folder is missing from your `PATH`, or only a runtime is installed.

### Install IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse
An IDE gives you code completion, refactoring and a debugger. IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition and Eclipse are both free. Create a new Java project, pick the JDK you installed as the "Project SDK", and the IDE will compile and run for you. Still learn the terminal commands: build servers and Docker images do not have an IDE.

### JDK vs JRE vs JVM

| Component | What it contains | Who needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JVM (Java Virtual Machine) | The engine that loads and executes bytecode, manages memory and garbage collection | Every machine that runs Java |
| JRE (Java Runtime Environment) | JVM + core class libraries needed to run programs | Users who only run Java apps |
| JDK (Java Development Kit) | JRE + developer tools: `javac`, `jar`, `javadoc`, `jshell`, debugger | Developers |

In short: **JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM**. Modern JDK distributions no longer ship a separate JRE download, but the concept still explains what each layer does.

## Your first Java program
Create a file named `Hello.java`. The file name must match the public class name.

```java
public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
```

```bash
javac Hello.java     # creates Hello.class (bytecode)
java Hello           # runs it - note: no .class extension
```

Output:

```
Hello, Java!
```

Line by line: `public class Hello` declares a class; `public static void main(String[] args)` is the entry point the JVM looks for; `System.out.println` prints a line to standard output.

## Variables, data types and operators
### Variables
A variable is a named storage location with a type: `int age = 25;`. Since Java 10 you can use `var` for local variables when the type is obvious from the right-hand side: `var name = "Asha";` (still statically typed as `String`).

### Primitive data types

| Type | Size | Example | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `byte` | 8 bit | `byte b = 100;` | raw binary data |
| `short` | 16 bit | `short s = 3000;` | rarely used |
| `int` | 32 bit | `int count = 42;` | whole numbers (default choice) |
| `long` | 64 bit | `long views = 9_000_000_000L;` | large whole numbers, timestamps |
| `float` | 32 bit | `float f = 3.14f;` | rarely used |
| `double` | 64 bit | `double price = 19.99;` | fractional numbers (default choice) |
| `char` | 16 bit | `char grade = 'A';` | a single UTF-16 character |
| `boolean` | true/false | `boolean active = true;` | conditions |

Everything else (such as `String`, arrays and your own classes) is a **reference type**: the variable holds a reference to an object on the heap.

### Operators
- Arithmetic: `+ - * / %` (`%` is remainder)
- Comparison: `== != < > <= >=`
- Logical: `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not) - `&&` and `||` short-circuit
- Assignment: `= += -= *= /=`; increment/decrement: `++ --`
- Ternary: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`

Watch integer division: `7 / 2` is `3` because both operands are `int`. Write `7 / 2.0` or `(double) 7 / 2` to get `3.5`.

```java
int a = 7, b = 2;
System.out.println(a / b);          // 3
System.out.println(a % b);          // 1
System.out.println((double) a / b); // 3.5
String result = a > b ? "a wins" : "b wins";
System.out.println(result);         // a wins
```

## Input and output
### Output
`System.out.println` prints with a newline, `System.out.print` without one, and `System.out.printf` formats: `System.out.printf("Total: %.2f%n", 12.5);` prints `Total: 12.50`.

### Command-line arguments
Values typed after the class name arrive in the `args` array.

```java
public class Greet {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length == 0) {
            System.out.println("Usage: java Greet <name>");
            return;
        }
        System.out.println("Hello, " + args[0]);
    }
}
```

Running `java Greet Ravi` prints `Hello, Ravi`. Always check `args.length` before indexing.

### The Scanner class
`Scanner` reads typed input from the keyboard (or a file).

```java
import java.util.Scanner;

public class AddTwo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("First number: ");
        int x = in.nextInt();
        System.out.print("Second number: ");
        int y = in.nextInt();
        System.out.println("Sum = " + (x + y));
    }
}
```

Note: after `nextInt()`, the newline is still in the buffer, so a following `nextLine()` returns an empty string. Call an extra `in.nextLine()` to consume it.

## Control flow and methods
### Conditions and loops
```java
int score = 82;
if (score >= 90) System.out.println("A");
else if (score >= 75) System.out.println("B");   // prints B
else System.out.println("C");

for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) System.out.print(i + " ");   // 1 2 3
int n = 3;
while (n > 0) { n--; }                                    // runs 3 times
```

Java also has `do-while` (runs at least once), `switch` (including the modern arrow form `case 1 -> ...`), `break` and `continue`.

### Methods
A method is a named, reusable block with parameters and a return type.

```java
static int square(int x) {
    return x * x;
}

static double average(int[] values) {
    if (values.length == 0) return 0;
    int sum = 0;
    for (int v : values) sum += v;
    return (double) sum / values.length;
}
```

Java is **pass-by-value**: a method receives a copy of each argument. For objects the copy is a copy of the reference, so the method can change the object's contents but cannot make the caller's variable point to a different object. Methods can be **overloaded**: same name, different parameter lists.

## Arrays, strings and wrapper classes
### Arrays
An array has a fixed length and zero-based indexes.

```java
int[] marks = {70, 85, 92};
System.out.println(marks.length);   // 3
System.out.println(marks[0]);       // 70
// marks[3] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
int[][] grid = new int[2][3];       // 2 rows, 3 columns, all 0
```

Use `java.util.Arrays` helpers: `Arrays.sort(marks)`, `Arrays.toString(marks)`.

### Strings
`String` objects are **immutable**: methods return new strings.

```java
String s = "  Java Full Stack ";
System.out.println(s.trim());                 // "Java Full Stack"
System.out.println(s.trim().toUpperCase());   // "JAVA FULL STACK"
System.out.println("java".equals("JAVA"));    // false
System.out.println("java".equalsIgnoreCase("JAVA")); // true
```

Compare text with `equals`, never `==` (which compares references). For building strings in loops, use `StringBuilder`:

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) sb.append(i).append(',');
System.out.println(sb);   // 0,1,2,
```

### Wrapper classes
Each primitive has a wrapper class: `int` → `Integer`, `double` → `Double`, `char` → `Character`, `boolean` → `Boolean`, and so on. Collections can only hold objects, so Java converts automatically (**autoboxing** and **unboxing**):

```java
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(5);                         // autoboxing int -> Integer
int first = nums.get(0);             // unboxing Integer -> int
int parsed = Integer.parseInt("42"); // String -> int
```

Beware: unboxing a `null` wrapper throws `NullPointerException`, and comparing two `Integer` objects with `==` compares references - use `equals`.

## Common mistakes
- File name does not match the public class name, so `javac` reports an error.
- Running `java Hello.class` instead of `java Hello`.
- Integer division silently dropping the fraction.
- Comparing strings with `==`.
- Accessing `args[0]` or `array[length]` without checking the length.

## Practice exercise
1. Write `GradeCalculator.java` that reads five marks with `Scanner`, stores them in an array and prints the total, the average with two decimals, and the highest mark.
2. Print a letter grade using `if/else if` (A ≥ 90, B ≥ 75, C ≥ 50, otherwise F).
3. Move the average calculation into a method `static double average(int[] marks)` and reject an empty array.
4. Accept the student name as a command-line argument and print a formatted report using `printf`.

## Key takeaways
- The JDK compiles (`javac`), the JVM runs bytecode (`java`).
- Choose `int`/`long` for whole numbers and `double` for fractions; watch integer division.
- Strings are immutable - compare with `equals`, build with `StringBuilder`.
- Arrays have fixed length and zero-based indexes.
- Wrapper classes let primitives live in collections through autoboxing.

lessons.title: Collections Framework
lessons.description: Section 1 · Programming Fundamentals. Choose List, Set, Queue or Map from the access pattern required.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Choose List, Set, Queue or Map from the access pattern required.
- Iterate over and modify collections safely with cursors.
- Sort with Comparable and Comparator and use the Collections utility class.

## Introduction to the Collections Framework
Arrays have a fixed size and few helper methods. The **Java Collections Framework** (package `java.util`) provides resizable data structures behind a small set of interfaces, so you can change the implementation without rewriting the code that uses it.

```
Iterable
└── Collection
    ├── List   (ordered, allows duplicates)   → ArrayList, LinkedList
    ├── Set    (no duplicates)                → HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet
    └── Queue  (processing order)             → ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue, LinkedList
Map (key → value, not a Collection)           → HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap
```

**Program to the interface:** declare `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` so you can swap in another `List` later.

## The List interface
A `List` keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and supports index access.

```java
List<String> skills = new ArrayList<>();
skills.add("Java");
skills.add("SQL");
skills.add("Java");               // duplicates allowed
skills.add(1, "React");           // insert at index 1
System.out.println(skills);       // [Java, React, SQL, Java]
System.out.println(skills.get(2)); // SQL
skills.remove("SQL");
System.out.println(skills.size()); // 3
System.out.println(skills.contains("React")); // true
```

| Implementation | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ArrayList` | Fast random access `get(i)` | Inserting/removing in the middle shifts elements |
| `LinkedList` | Fast insert/remove at the ends | Slow `get(i)`; more memory per element |

Use `ArrayList` by default. `List.of(...)` creates an **immutable** list - calling `add` on it throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

## The Set interface
A `Set` stores unique elements.

```java
Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>(List.of("java", "spring", "java", "sql"));
System.out.println(tags.size());      // 3
System.out.println(tags.add("sql"));  // false - already present
```

| Implementation | Order | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HashSet` | No guaranteed order | Fast membership checks |
| `LinkedHashSet` | Insertion order | Unique items, predictable display |
| `TreeSet` | Sorted (natural or comparator) | Sorted unique items, range queries |

Hash-based sets rely on `equals` and `hashCode`. If you put your own objects in a `HashSet` or use them as `HashMap` keys, override **both** consistently: equal objects must have equal hash codes.

## The Queue interface
A `Queue` holds elements waiting to be processed.

```java
Queue<String> tickets = new ArrayDeque<>();
tickets.offer("T1");
tickets.offer("T2");
System.out.println(tickets.peek()); // T1 (look, do not remove)
System.out.println(tickets.poll()); // T1 (remove)
System.out.println(tickets);        // [T2]

Queue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 3));
System.out.println(pq.poll());      // 1 - smallest first
```

- `ArrayDeque` works as a FIFO queue **and** as a stack (`push`/`pop`) - prefer it over the legacy `Stack` class.
- `PriorityQueue` always returns the smallest (or highest-priority) element first.
- `offer`/`poll`/`peek` return `false`/`null` on failure; `add`/`remove`/`element` throw exceptions.

## The Map interface
A `Map` associates unique keys with values.

```java
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
stock.put("laptop", 5);
stock.put("mouse", 20);
stock.put("laptop", 7);                     // replaces the old value
System.out.println(stock.get("laptop"));    // 7
System.out.println(stock.getOrDefault("pen", 0)); // 0
stock.merge("mouse", 5, Integer::sum);      // 25

for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : stock.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + " -> " + e.getValue());
}
```

| Implementation | Order | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HashMap` | None | Fastest general choice; allows one `null` key |
| `LinkedHashMap` | Insertion (or access) order | Useful for LRU caches |
| `TreeMap` | Sorted by key | `firstKey`, `headMap`, `ceilingKey` |

### Word-count example
```java
String text = "to be or not to be";
Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>();
for (String w : text.split(" ")) counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
System.out.println(counts);   // {be=2, not=1, or=1, to=2}
```

## Cursors: Iterator, ListIterator and Enumeration
A **cursor** walks through a collection one element at a time.

```java
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
Iterator<Integer> it = nums.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next() % 2 == 0) it.remove();   // safe removal
}
System.out.println(nums);   // [1, 3, 5]
```

- `Iterator` - forward only, supports `remove()`; works with every collection.
- `ListIterator` - for lists; moves forward and backward, supports `add` and `set`.
- `Enumeration` - legacy cursor for `Vector`/`Hashtable`; read only.

Removing elements inside a for-each loop with `list.remove(x)` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `iterator.remove()` or `list.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0)`.

## Comparable and Comparator
### Comparable - natural ordering
A class implements `Comparable<T>` and its `compareTo` method to define its default order (negative = before, zero = equal, positive = after).

```java
record Student(String name, int marks) implements Comparable<Student> {
    public int compareTo(Student other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.marks, other.marks);
    }
}
List<Student> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
    new Student("Asha", 88), new Student("Ravi", 72), new Student("Mei", 95)));
Collections.sort(list);   // by marks ascending
```

### Comparator - external orderings
A `Comparator` defines an ordering outside the class, so you can have many.

```java
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Student::name));                    // by name
list.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::marks).reversed());     // highest marks first
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Student::marks)
                    .thenComparing(Student::name));                // tie-break by name
```

| Comparable | Comparator |
| --- | --- |
| `java.lang`, method `compareTo(T o)` | `java.util`, method `compare(T a, T b)` |
| One natural order, inside the class | Many orders, outside the class |
| Changes the class | Works for classes you cannot modify |

## The Collections utility class
`java.util.Collections` (note the "s") holds static helpers:

```java
List<Integer> n = new ArrayList<>(List.of(4, 1, 3));
Collections.sort(n);                       // [1, 3, 4]
Collections.reverse(n);                    // [4, 3, 1]
Collections.shuffle(n);
System.out.println(Collections.max(n));    // 4
System.out.println(Collections.frequency(List.of("a","b","a"), "a")); // 2
List<Integer> ro = Collections.unmodifiableList(n);   // read-only view
```

## Common mistakes
- Using `List` when you need fast lookup by key - use a `Map`.
- Custom objects in a `HashSet` without `equals`/`hashCode`, leading to duplicates.
- Modifying a list inside a for-each loop.
- Calling `add` on `List.of(...)`.
- Assuming `HashMap` iteration order is stable.

## Practice exercise
1. Build a `Library` class with `Map<String, Book>` keyed by ISBN and a `Set<String>` of genres.
2. Keep a `Queue<String>` of members waiting for a borrowed book; serve them in FIFO order.
3. Implement `Comparable<Book>` by title, then print books sorted by year (descending) using a `Comparator`.
4. Remove all books older than 2000 using an `Iterator` and then using `removeIf` - compare the code.

## Key takeaways
- List = ordered with duplicates, Set = unique, Queue = processing order, Map = key/value lookup.
- Program to interfaces; pick `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, `HashMap`, `ArrayDeque` by default.
- Override `equals` and `hashCode` together for hash-based collections.
- Use `Iterator.remove` or `removeIf` to remove while iterating.
- `Comparable` = one natural order; `Comparator` = any number of custom orders.

lessons.title: Java 8 Features
lessons.description: Section 1 · Programming Fundamentals. Write lambda expressions and method references for functional interfaces.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Write lambda expressions and method references for functional interfaces.
- Process collections declaratively with the Streams API and Collectors.
- Use Optional, the java.time API and default and static interface methods.

## Why Java 8 changed everything
Java 8 (2014) introduced functional programming features that every modern Java code base - including Spring Boot - relies on: lambdas, streams, `Optional`, the new Date/Time API and interface default methods. This module teaches each one with examples you will reuse in later modules.

## Lambda expressions
A **lambda** is an anonymous function: a short block of code you can pass around as a value.

Syntax: `(parameters) -> expression` or `(parameters) -> { statements; }`

```java
// Before Java 8: anonymous inner class
Comparator<String> byLength = new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.length() - b.length(); }
};

// With a lambda
Comparator<String> byLength2 = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ravi", "Mei", "Alexander"));
names.sort(byLength2);
System.out.println(names);   // [Mei, Ravi, Alexander]
```

Rules: parameter types are usually inferred; parentheses are optional for a single parameter (`x -> x * 2`); braces and `return` are needed for multiple statements. A lambda can use local variables from the enclosing scope only if they are **effectively final** (never reassigned).

## Functional interfaces
A lambda needs a target type: a **functional interface**, which has exactly one abstract method. Mark your own with `@FunctionalInterface` so the compiler enforces that.

```java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Discount {
    double apply(double price);
}
Discount festive = p -> p * 0.9;
System.out.println(festive.apply(1000));   // 900.0
```

The `java.util.function` package provides the common shapes:

| Interface | Method | Shape | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Predicate<T>` | `test(T)` | T → boolean | `s -> s.isEmpty()` |
| `Function<T,R>` | `apply(T)` | T → R | `s -> s.length()` |
| `Consumer<T>` | `accept(T)` | T → nothing | `s -> System.out.println(s)` |
| `Supplier<T>` | `get()` | nothing → T | `() -> new ArrayList<>()` |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T)` | T → T | `s -> s.trim()` |
| `BinaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T,T)` | (T,T) → T | `(a, b) -> a + b` |

They can be combined: `isLong.and(startsWithA)`, `trim.andThen(upper)`.

## Method references
When a lambda only calls an existing method, a **method reference** (`::`) is shorter.

| Kind | Syntax | Equivalent lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static method | `Integer::parseInt` | `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)` |
| Instance method of a particular object | `System.out::println` | `x -> System.out.println(x)` |
| Instance method of an arbitrary object | `String::toUpperCase` | `s -> s.toUpperCase()` |
| Constructor | `ArrayList::new` | `() -> new ArrayList<>()` |

```java
List.of("a", "b").forEach(System.out::println);
```

## Streams API
A **stream** is a pipeline that processes a sequence of elements declaratively: *what* you want, not *how* to loop. A pipeline has a **source**, zero or more **intermediate operations** (lazy) and one **terminal operation** (triggers execution).

```java
record Employee(String name, String dept, double salary) { }

List<Employee> staff = List.of(
    new Employee("Asha", "Engineering", 90000),
    new Employee("Ravi", "Sales", 50000),
    new Employee("Mei", "Engineering", 120000),
    new Employee("Omar", "Sales", 65000));

List<String> highEarners = staff.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.salary() > 60000)        // intermediate
    .map(Employee::name)                    // intermediate
    .sorted()                               // intermediate
    .toList();                              // terminal (Java 16+)
System.out.println(highEarners);   // [Asha, Mei, Omar]
```

Common operations:
- Intermediate: `filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek`
- Terminal: `forEach`, `collect`, `toList`, `count`, `sum` (on number streams), `min`/`max`, `reduce`, `anyMatch`/`allMatch`/`noneMatch`, `findFirst`

### Collectors
```java
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = staff.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));

Map<String, Double> avgSalary = staff.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept, Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)));
System.out.println(avgSalary);   // {Engineering=105000.0, Sales=57500.0}

double total = staff.stream().mapToDouble(Employee::salary).sum();      // 325000.0
String names = staff.stream().map(Employee::name).collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
```

Stream rules: a stream can be consumed only once; operations should not modify the source; keep lambdas free of side effects. `parallelStream()` can help CPU-heavy work on large data but adds overhead and must never write to shared non-thread-safe state.

## Optional class
`Optional<T>` is a container that may or may not hold a value. It makes "no result" explicit in a method's return type instead of returning `null`.

```java
Optional<Employee> top = staff.stream()
    .max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::salary));

System.out.println(top.map(Employee::name).orElse("nobody"));   // Mei

Optional<String> missing = Optional.empty();
missing.ifPresent(System.out::println);           // does nothing
String v = missing.orElseGet(() -> "default");     // lazily computed fallback
// missing.orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("Not found"));
```

Prefer `map`, `filter`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow` and `ifPresent` over calling `get()` (which throws if empty). Use `Optional` for return values, not for fields or method parameters.

## Date and Time API
The `java.time` package replaces the old mutable `Date` and `Calendar`. Its classes are **immutable** and thread-safe.

| Class | Represents | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LocalDate` | A date without time or zone | 2026-10-27 |
| `LocalTime` | A time without date | 14:30 |
| `LocalDateTime` | Date and time, no zone | 2026-10-27T14:30 |
| `ZonedDateTime` | Date, time and time zone | 2026-10-27T14:30+05:30[Asia/Kolkata] |
| `Instant` | A point on the UTC timeline | for timestamps and logs |
| `Duration` / `Period` | Time-based / date-based amount | `Duration.ofMinutes(90)`, `Period.ofDays(7)` |

```java
LocalDate joined = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 15);
LocalDate review = joined.plusMonths(6);
System.out.println(review);                                  // 2024-09-15
System.out.println(ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(joined, review)); // 184

DateTimeFormatter fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy");
System.out.println(review.format(fmt));                      // 15 Sep 2024
LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("2026-01-31");
```

Store timestamps as `Instant` (UTC) and convert to a user's zone only for display.

## Default and static methods in interfaces
Before Java 8, adding a method to an interface broke every implementing class. A **default method** has a body, so existing implementations inherit it automatically. A **static method** in an interface is a helper called on the interface itself.

```java
interface Greeter {
    String name();

    default String greet() {                 // inherited by all implementations
        return "Hello, " + name() + "!";
    }

    static Greeter of(String n) {            // factory helper
        return () -> n;
    }
}

System.out.println(Greeter.of("Asha").greet());   // Hello, Asha!
```

If a class implements two interfaces with the same default method, it must override the method and may pick one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

## Common mistakes
- Reassigning a local variable used inside a lambda (must be effectively final).
- Reusing a consumed stream (`IllegalStateException`).
- Forgetting a terminal operation, so nothing executes.
- Calling `Optional.get()` without checking.
- Using `LocalDateTime` for global timestamps instead of `Instant`.

## Practice exercise
Given a `List<Order>` where `Order(String customer, String category, double amount, LocalDate date)`:
1. Print the total revenue.
2. Find the top three orders by amount.
3. Group revenue by category with `Collectors.groupingBy` and `summingDouble`.
4. Find the first order above 10,000 as an `Optional` and print "none" if absent.
5. List distinct customers who ordered in the last 30 days, sorted alphabetically.
6. Write a functional interface `TaxRule` and two lambda implementations.

## Key takeaways
- Lambdas implement functional interfaces concisely; method references are even shorter.
- Streams express data processing as filter/map/collect pipelines.
- `Optional` makes absence explicit - avoid bare `get()`.
- `java.time` types are immutable; pick the one that matches the meaning of your data.
- Default methods let interfaces evolve without breaking implementations.

A class that contains only static methods
Which stream operation keeps only matching elements?
Which java.time class represents a date without a time?

lessons.title: DBMS
lessons.description: Section 2 · Database Fundamentals. Explain what a DBMS provides over plain files, including ACID transactions.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Explain what a DBMS provides over plain files, including ACID transactions.
- Identify keys and model entities and relationships with an ER diagram.
- Normalise a table design to third normal form.

## Introduction to DBMS
A **database** is an organised collection of data. A **Database Management System (DBMS)** is the software that stores that data and lets many users and applications read and change it safely. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server (relational) and MongoDB (document).

Why not just use files?

| Plain files | DBMS |
| --- | --- |
| Duplicate data across files becomes inconsistent | Shared, centrally defined data |
| Each program writes its own search code | Declarative query language (SQL) |
| Concurrent writes overwrite each other | Concurrency control and locking |
| Crashes can leave half-written data | Transactions and recovery |
| Access control is all-or-nothing | Users, roles and privileges |

A **Relational DBMS (RDBMS)** stores data in **tables** (relations) made of **rows** (records/tuples) and **columns** (attributes). Each column has a data type and optional constraints.

### ACID transactions
Relational databases guarantee **ACID** properties for transactions:
- **Atomicity** - all statements in a transaction succeed, or none do.
- **Consistency** - a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another (constraints hold).
- **Isolation** - concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work.
- **Durability** - once committed, data survives crashes.

## Database schema
A **schema** is the blueprint of the database: tables, columns, types, relationships and constraints. It is described with DDL (Data Definition Language, Module 10).

Levels of abstraction:
- **Physical level** - how data is stored on disk (files, pages, indexes).
- **Logical (conceptual) level** - tables, columns and relationships; what developers design.
- **View (external) level** - what particular users see, for example a view hiding salary columns.

This separation gives **data independence**: you can add an index (physical) without changing queries, or add a column (logical) without breaking existing views.

## Keys
Keys identify rows and connect tables.

| Key | Definition | Example in `employee` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Super key | Any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row | `{emp_id, name}` |
| Candidate key | A minimal super key (no extra columns) | `emp_id`, `email` |
| Primary key | The candidate key chosen as the main identifier; unique and NOT NULL | `emp_id` |
| Alternate key | Candidate keys not chosen as primary | `email` |
| Composite key | A key made of two or more columns | `(student_id, course_id)` in enrollment |
| Foreign key | A column referencing another table's primary key | `dept_id` → `department.dept_id` |

A **surrogate key** is an artificial identifier (an auto-increment number or UUID); a **natural key** has business meaning (email, ISBN). Surrogate keys are usually preferred as primary keys because business values can change.

## ER diagrams
An **Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram** models the data before you create tables.
- **Entity** (rectangle): a thing you store data about - Student, Course.
- **Attribute** (oval): a property - name, email. Key attributes are underlined; multivalued attributes have double ovals; derived attributes (age from date of birth) have dashed ovals.
- **Relationship** (diamond): how entities relate - Student *enrolls in* Course.
- **Cardinality**: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:N), many-to-many (M:N).
- **Participation**: total (every entity must participate) or partial.

```
[Department] 1 ──< works in >── N [Employee]
[Student]    M ──< enrolls  >── N [Course]
```

### From ER to tables
- Each entity becomes a table; its key becomes the primary key.
- **1:N** - put a foreign key on the "many" side (`employee.dept_id`).
- **M:N** - create a **junction table** with both foreign keys (`enrollment(student_id, course_id, enrolled_on)`).
- **1:1** - put a unique foreign key on one side, or merge the tables.

## Database design
A good design process:
1. Collect requirements and business rules ("an employee belongs to exactly one department").
2. Identify entities, attributes and relationships; draw the ER diagram.
3. Convert the diagram to tables, keys and constraints.
4. Normalise (next section) to remove redundancy.
5. Add indexes for the queries you expect to run.
6. Review with sample data and edge cases.

Naming tips: use singular or plural consistently (`employee` or `employees`), `snake_case`, and an `id` or `<table>_id` primary key.

## Normalization
**Normalization** organises tables to reduce duplicated data and prevent **anomalies**:
- *Insert anomaly* - cannot add a department until it has an employee.
- *Update anomaly* - a department name stored in 500 rows must be changed 500 times.
- *Delete anomaly* - deleting the last employee also deletes the department's information.

Starting table:

| order_id | customer | customer_city | products |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Asha | Pune | Pen, Book |
| 2 | Asha | Pune | Bag |

### First Normal Form (1NF)
Every column holds **atomic** values - no lists, no repeating groups. Split "Pen, Book" into separate rows (`order_item` table).

### Second Normal Form (2NF)
1NF, and every non-key column depends on the **whole** primary key (no partial dependency). In `order_item(order_id, product_id, product_name, qty)`, `product_name` depends only on `product_id` - move it to a `product` table.

### Third Normal Form (3NF)
2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no **transitive** dependency). `customer_city` depends on `customer`, not on the order - move it to a `customer` table.

### BCNF
Boyce-Codd Normal Form tightens 3NF: for every functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key.

Result:

```
customer(customer_id PK, name, city)
orders(order_id PK, customer_id FK, order_date)
product(product_id PK, name, price)
order_item(order_id FK, product_id FK, qty, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, product_id))
```

**Denormalization** deliberately adds redundancy for read performance (for example, storing an order total). Do it only with a measured reason and a plan to keep copies consistent.

## Common mistakes
- Storing comma-separated lists in a single column.
- Using a changeable natural value (email, phone) as the primary key.
- Modelling a many-to-many relationship without a junction table.
- Copying descriptive data (department name) into every row.

## Practice exercise
Design the database for a training portal:
1. Entities: Employee, Department, Course, Trainer, Enrollment.
2. Draw the ER diagram with cardinalities (an employee can enroll in many courses; a course has one trainer).
3. Convert it to tables with primary keys, foreign keys and a composite key for enrollment.
4. Take this flat table and normalise it to 3NF: `(emp_id, emp_name, dept_name, dept_head, course_code, course_title, score)`.

## Key takeaways
- A DBMS provides shared, consistent, concurrent and recoverable data access; RDBMSs guarantee ACID.
- Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys enforce relationships.
- ER diagrams capture entities, attributes and cardinalities before you write SQL.
- M:N relationships need a junction table.
- Normalise to 3NF to eliminate anomalies; denormalise only deliberately.
quiz: Which key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL?
How is a many-to-many relationship represented in tables?
A junction table with two foreign keys
A single foreign key on one side
What does the A in ACID stand for?

lessons.title: SQL
lessons.description: Section 2 · Database Fundamentals. Write CRUD statements with constraints that protect data integrity.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Write CRUD statements with constraints that protect data integrity.
- Combine tables with joins, aggregates, subqueries and views.
- Use indexes, stored procedures, triggers and transactions appropriately.

## SQL overview
**SQL (Structured Query Language)** is the standard language for relational databases. Its statements fall into groups:

| Group | Purpose | Statements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DDL - Data Definition | Define structure | `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` |
| DML - Data Manipulation | Change data | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` |
| DQL - Data Query | Read data | `SELECT` |
| DCL - Data Control | Permissions | `GRANT`, `REVOKE` |
| TCL - Transaction Control | Transactions | `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT` |

The examples in this module use this schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE department (
    dept_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name      VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE employee (
    emp_id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email     VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE,
    salary    DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),
    dept_id   INT,
    joined_on DATE DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),
    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES department(dept_id)
);
```

## CRUD operations
**C**reate, **R**ead, **U**pdate, **D**elete - the four basic operations behind every application screen.

```sql
-- Create
INSERT INTO department (dept_id, name) VALUES (1, 'Engineering'), (2, 'Sales'), (3, 'HR');
INSERT INTO employee (emp_id, name, email, salary, dept_id)
VALUES (101, 'Asha', 'asha@corp.com', 90000, 1),
       (102, 'Ravi', 'ravi@corp.com', 50000, 2),
       (103, 'Mei',  'mei@corp.com', 120000, 1),
       (104, 'Omar', 'omar@corp.com', 65000, NULL);

-- Read
SELECT name, salary FROM employee WHERE salary > 60000 ORDER BY salary DESC;
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE name LIKE 'A%';           -- starts with A
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE dept_id IN (1, 2);
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE dept_id IS NULL;           -- never "= NULL"
SELECT name FROM employee ORDER BY name LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0;

-- Update (always with WHERE!)
UPDATE employee SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_id = 1;

-- Delete (always with WHERE!)
DELETE FROM employee WHERE emp_id = 104;
```

`DELETE` removes chosen rows and can be rolled back; `TRUNCATE` removes all rows quickly; `DROP` removes the table itself.

## Constraints
Constraints let the database enforce business rules no matter which application writes the data.

| Constraint | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `PRIMARY KEY` | Unique and not null; identifies each row |
| `FOREIGN KEY` | Value must exist in the referenced table (or be NULL) |
| `UNIQUE` | No two rows share the value |
| `NOT NULL` | A value is required |
| `CHECK` | A boolean condition must hold (`salary > 0`) |
| `DEFAULT` | Value used when none is supplied |

Foreign keys can specify what happens when the parent row changes: `ON DELETE CASCADE` (delete children), `ON DELETE SET NULL`, or the default `RESTRICT` (refuse).

## Joins
Joins combine rows from related tables.

```sql
-- INNER JOIN: only employees that have a matching department
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employee e
INNER JOIN department d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id;
-- Asha | Engineering, Ravi | Sales, Mei | Engineering

-- LEFT JOIN: all employees, department or NULL
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employee e
LEFT JOIN department d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id;
-- ... plus Omar | NULL

-- Departments with no employees
SELECT d.name
FROM department d
LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
WHERE e.emp_id IS NULL;            -- HR
```

| Join | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `INNER JOIN` | Rows with a match in both tables |
| `LEFT JOIN` | All rows from the left table, matches or NULL from the right |
| `RIGHT JOIN` | All rows from the right table |
| `FULL OUTER JOIN` | All rows from both (not in MySQL; emulate with `UNION`) |
| `CROSS JOIN` | Every combination (Cartesian product) |
| Self join | A table joined to itself, e.g. employee and manager |

## Aggregation and functions
```sql
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS headcount, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_salary
FROM department d
LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) > 0
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
```

- **Aggregate functions**: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`.
- `WHERE` filters rows **before** grouping; `HAVING` filters groups **after** aggregation.
- **Scalar functions**: `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `CONCAT`, `LENGTH`, `SUBSTRING`, `ROUND`, `COALESCE(x, default)`, `NOW()`, `DATEDIFF`.
- **Window functions** (`OVER`) compute values across related rows without collapsing them: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)`.

Logical order of evaluation: `FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`.

## Subqueries
A subquery is a query nested inside another.

```sql
-- Employees earning more than the company average
SELECT name, salary FROM employee
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee);

-- Employees in departments named 'Engineering' or 'Sales'
SELECT name FROM employee
WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM department WHERE name IN ('Engineering', 'Sales'));

-- Correlated subquery: earns more than their own department's average
SELECT e.name FROM employee e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employee x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id);

-- EXISTS: departments that have at least one employee
SELECT d.name FROM department d
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id);
```

## Views, stored procedures and triggers
### Views
A **view** is a saved query that behaves like a virtual table. Use it to simplify complex joins or hide sensitive columns.

```sql
CREATE VIEW employee_directory AS
SELECT e.name, e.email, d.name AS department
FROM employee e LEFT JOIN department d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id;

SELECT * FROM employee_directory WHERE department = 'Sales';
```

### Stored procedures
A **stored procedure** is named SQL logic stored in the database and called with parameters (MySQL syntax):

```sql
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE give_raise(IN p_dept INT, IN p_percent DECIMAL(5,2))
BEGIN
    UPDATE employee SET salary = salary * (1 + p_percent / 100) WHERE dept_id = p_dept;
END //
DELIMITER ;

CALL give_raise(1, 5);
```

### Triggers
A **trigger** runs automatically before or after `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` on a table - for example, an audit log:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER salary_audit
AFTER UPDATE ON employee
FOR EACH ROW
INSERT INTO salary_log(emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_at)
VALUES (OLD.emp_id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, NOW());
```

Keep most business logic in the application where it is easier to test and version; use procedures and triggers for focused database-level needs.

## Indexing
An **index** is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table - like the index at the back of a book.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_employee_dept ON employee(dept_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_employee_email ON employee(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept_salary ON employee(dept_id, salary);   -- composite
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1;                -- shows the plan
```

- Index columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `ORDER BY`.
- A composite index `(a, b)` helps queries on `a` or on `a and b`, but not on `b` alone (leftmost-prefix rule).
- Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and use storage - do not index everything.
- Primary keys and unique constraints are indexed automatically.

## Transactions
A **transaction** groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;            -- both changes become permanent
-- If anything fails: ROLLBACK;  -- undo both
```

`SAVEPOINT name` marks a point you can `ROLLBACK TO`. **Isolation levels** control what concurrent transactions see: `READ UNCOMMITTED` (dirty reads possible), `READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ` (MySQL InnoDB default) and `SERIALIZABLE` (strictest, slowest).

## Common mistakes
- `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `WHERE`.
- Comparing with `= NULL` instead of `IS NULL`.
- Selecting non-aggregated columns that are not in `GROUP BY`.
- Using `WHERE` to filter aggregates (use `HAVING`).
- Building SQL by concatenating user input (SQL injection - Module 13 shows the fix).

## Practice exercise
Using the employee/department schema:
1. List each department with its headcount, including departments with zero employees.
2. Find the second-highest salary (two ways: subquery and `LIMIT/OFFSET`).
3. Create a view `high_earners` for salaries above the company average.
4. Write a transaction that moves an employee to another department and logs the move; roll it back if the department does not exist.
5. Add an index that helps `WHERE dept_id = ? ORDER BY salary DESC` and check it with `EXPLAIN`.

## Key takeaways
- SQL is grouped into DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL.
- Constraints enforce rules in the database itself.
- `INNER JOIN` keeps matches; `LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row.
- `WHERE` filters rows, `HAVING` filters groups.
- Indexes speed reads at a write cost; transactions make multi-step changes atomic.
quiz: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
Which join returns all rows from the left table even without a match?
How do you test whether a column has no value?

lessons.title: MySQL
lessons.description: Section 2 · Database Fundamentals. Install MySQL, create a least-privilege application user and work with MySQL Workbench.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Install MySQL, create a least-privilege application user and work with MySQL Workbench.
- Create databases and tables with appropriate MySQL data types and constraints.
- Perform CRUD and aggregation and analyse index use with EXPLAIN.

## Introduction to MySQL
**MySQL** is one of the most widely used open-source relational databases. It powers web applications from small blogs to very large platforms and is the default choice in many Java/Spring Boot projects. Its default storage engine, **InnoDB**, supports transactions, foreign keys and row-level locking.

## Installation
1. Download **MySQL Community Server** for your OS (Windows users can use the MySQL Installer, which also installs Workbench). On macOS use the DMG or `brew install mysql`; on Ubuntu `sudo apt install mysql-server`. Docker users can run `docker run --name mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=secret -p 3306:3306 -d mysql:8`.
2. During setup choose a strong **root password** and keep the default port **3306**.
3. Verify from a terminal:

```bash
mysql --version
mysql -u root -p          # prompts for the password, opens the mysql> shell
```

Inside the shell:

```sql
SHOW DATABASES;
SELECT VERSION();
EXIT;
```

### Create an application user
Never connect your application as `root`. Create a user with only the privileges it needs:

```sql
CREATE USER 'lms_app'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'Str0ng!Passw0rd';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON training_db.* TO 'lms_app'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
```

## MySQL Workbench
**MySQL Workbench** is the official graphical tool. With it you can:
- Create saved **connections** (host, port, user) and open SQL editor tabs.
- Browse schemas, tables and columns in the Navigator panel.
- Run queries (lightning-bolt icon or Ctrl+Enter for the current statement) and view results in a grid.
- Design tables with a form instead of typing DDL.
- Draw **EER diagrams** and reverse-engineer an existing database into a diagram.
- Inspect query plans (Explain) and server status.
- Export and import data (Server → Data Export / Data Import).

Other good clients: DBeaver, the IntelliJ IDEA Database tool, and the command-line `mysql` client.

## Creating databases and tables
```sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS training_db
  CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE training_db;

CREATE TABLE trainer (
    id          INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name   VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email       VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE course (
    id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    code         VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    title        VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    fee          DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (fee >= 0),
    level        ENUM('BEGINNER','INTERMEDIATE','ADVANCED') DEFAULT 'BEGINNER',
    trainer_id   INT,
    published    BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_course_trainer FOREIGN KEY (trainer_id)
        REFERENCES trainer(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

SHOW TABLES;
DESCRIBE course;
```

Useful MySQL data types:

| Type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `INT`, `BIGINT` | Whole numbers, IDs |
| `DECIMAL(p,s)` | Money - exact, never `FLOAT` for currency |
| `VARCHAR(n)` / `TEXT` | Short / long text |
| `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP` | Dates and times (`TIMESTAMP` is stored in UTC) |
| `BOOLEAN` | Alias of `TINYINT(1)` |
| `ENUM(...)` | One value from a fixed list |
| `JSON` | Semi-structured data with JSON functions |

Use `utf8mb4` so names and emoji in every language are stored correctly. Changing a table later: `ALTER TABLE course ADD COLUMN duration_hours INT;`, `ALTER TABLE course MODIFY title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL;`, `ALTER TABLE course DROP COLUMN published;`.

## CRUD in MySQL
```sql
INSERT INTO trainer (full_name, email) VALUES ('Kiran Rao', 'kiran@corp.com');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();                         -- id generated by AUTO_INCREMENT

INSERT INTO course (code, title, fee, level, trainer_id)
VALUES ('JAVA101', 'Java Basics', 4999, 'BEGINNER', 1),
       ('SPR201', 'Spring Boot', 7999, 'INTERMEDIATE', 1);

SELECT code, title, fee FROM course WHERE level = 'BEGINNER';
UPDATE course SET published = TRUE WHERE code = 'JAVA101';
DELETE FROM course WHERE code = 'SPR201';

-- Insert or update in one statement ("upsert")
INSERT INTO course (code, title, fee) VALUES ('JAVA101', 'Java Basics', 5499)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE fee = VALUES(fee);
```

MySQL Workbench runs in **safe update mode** by default, refusing `UPDATE`/`DELETE` without a key in `WHERE` - a useful guard.

## Indexes in MySQL
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_course_level ON course(level);
CREATE INDEX idx_course_trainer_level ON course(trainer_id, level);
SHOW INDEX FROM course;

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM course WHERE trainer_id = 1 AND level = 'BEGINNER';
DROP INDEX idx_course_level ON course;
```

In `EXPLAIN` output, check `type` (`ALL` means a full table scan, `ref`/`range`/`const` are better), `key` (the index chosen) and `rows` (estimated rows read). InnoDB stores rows ordered by primary key (the **clustered index**); secondary indexes point back to the primary key, so keep primary keys short. `FULLTEXT` indexes support natural-language search on text columns.

## Aggregation
```sql
SELECT level,
       COUNT(*)            AS courses,
       ROUND(AVG(fee), 2)  AS avg_fee,
       MAX(fee)            AS max_fee
FROM course
GROUP BY level
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1
ORDER BY avg_fee DESC;

-- Subtotals and a grand total
SELECT level, SUM(fee) FROM course GROUP BY level WITH ROLLUP;

-- Comma-separated list per group
SELECT t.full_name, GROUP_CONCAT(c.code ORDER BY c.code SEPARATOR ', ') AS courses
FROM trainer t LEFT JOIN course c ON c.trainer_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id, t.full_name;
```

MySQL 8 also supports window functions (`ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `SUM() OVER (...)`) and common table expressions (`WITH ... AS (...)`), which make reports much easier to read.

## Backups and operations basics
- Export a database: `mysqldump -u root -p training_db > training_db.sql`
- Restore it: `mysql -u root -p training_db < training_db.sql`
- Test restores regularly - a backup you have never restored is not proven.
- Keep credentials out of source code (environment variables or a secrets manager).

## Common mistakes
- Using `root` from the application.
- Storing money as `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE`.
- Using the legacy `utf8` charset instead of `utf8mb4`.
- Forgetting `ENGINE=InnoDB` on very old servers (no transactions with MyISAM).
- Adding indexes without checking `EXPLAIN`.

## Practice exercise
1. Install MySQL and Workbench; create `training_db` with `utf8mb4`.
2. Create `trainer`, `course`, `employee` and `enrollment` tables with keys and constraints.
3. Insert at least 5 courses and 10 enrollments.
4. Write queries: courses per level, average fee per trainer, employees enrolled in more than two courses.
5. Add an index for "enrollments by employee ordered by date" and compare `EXPLAIN` before and after.
6. Back up the database with `mysqldump` and restore it into `training_db_copy`.

## Key takeaways
- MySQL with InnoDB provides transactions, foreign keys and row-level locking.
- Use Workbench (or another client) to explore schemas, run queries and draw diagrams.
- Choose correct types: `DECIMAL` for money, `utf8mb4` for text, `AUTO_INCREMENT` keys.

lessons.title: MongoDB
lessons.description: Section 2 · Database Fundamentals. Compare SQL and NoSQL data models and choose between them.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Compare SQL and NoSQL data models and choose between them.
- Model documents with embedding or references and perform CRUD with the MongoDB query API.
- Build aggregation pipelines and design indexes from query patterns.

## NoSQL basics
**NoSQL** ("not only SQL") databases store data in models other than relational tables. They became popular for flexible schemas, horizontal scaling and specific access patterns.

| NoSQL type | Data model | Examples | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Document | JSON-like documents | MongoDB, Couchbase | Catalogues, profiles, content |
| Key-value | Key → value | Redis, DynamoDB | Caching, sessions |
| Column-family | Wide rows grouped in column families | Cassandra, HBase | Huge write volumes, time series |
| Graph | Nodes and edges | Neo4j | Social networks, recommendations |

**MongoDB** is the most popular document database. It stores data as **BSON** (binary JSON) documents inside **collections**, inside **databases**.

## SQL vs NoSQL

| | SQL (relational) | NoSQL (MongoDB) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Tables with a fixed schema | Collections of flexible documents |
| Relationships | Joins and foreign keys | Embedding or references (`$lookup`) |
| Scaling | Usually vertical; sharding is harder | Built-in horizontal sharding |
| Transactions | Strong ACID across tables | Atomic per document; multi-document transactions available |
| Query language | SQL | MongoDB Query API (JSON-style) |
| Best for | Complex relationships, strict integrity (banking, orders) | Rapidly changing structure, nested data, high scale |

| Relational term | MongoDB term |
| --- | --- |
| Database | Database |
| Table | Collection |
| Row | Document |
| Column | Field |
| Primary key | `_id` field (auto-generated `ObjectId`) |
| Join | Embedding or `$lookup` |

Many systems use both: SQL for orders and payments, MongoDB for a product catalogue or activity feed.

## Installation
- Install **MongoDB Community Server** from the official site, or run `docker run -d --name mongo -p 27017:27017 mongo:7`.
- Install **mongosh**, the MongoDB shell, and optionally **MongoDB Compass**, the GUI.
- Cloud option: a free **MongoDB Atlas** cluster.

```bash
mongosh                               # connects to mongodb://localhost:27017
```

```javascript
show dbs
use training                          // switches (creates on first write)
db.getName()
```

## Collections and documents
A document is a set of field-value pairs, and values can be nested documents or arrays:

```javascript
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  code: "JAVA101",
  title: "Java Basics",
  fee: 4999,
  tags: ["java", "beginner"],
  trainer: { name: "Kiran Rao", email: "kiran@corp.com" },
  modules: [ { no: 1, title: "Syntax" }, { no: 2, title: "OOP" } ],
  published: true
}
```

Collections are created automatically on first insert, or explicitly with validation rules - flexible does not mean "no rules":

```javascript
db.createCollection("courses", {
  validator: { $jsonSchema: {
    bsonType: "object",
    required: ["code", "title", "fee"],
    properties: {
      code:  { bsonType: "string" },
      fee:   { bsonType: ["int", "double", "decimal"], minimum: 0 }
    }
  }}
})
```

### Embedding vs referencing
- **Embed** data that is read together and bounded in size (a course's modules, an order's line items).
- **Reference** (store another document's `_id`) when data is shared, changes independently or can grow without limit (all enrollments of a popular course).

## CRUD operations
```javascript
// Create
db.courses.insertOne({ code: "JAVA101", title: "Java Basics", fee: 4999, tags: ["java"], published: true })
db.courses.insertMany([
  { code: "SPR201", title: "Spring Boot", fee: 7999, tags: ["java", "spring"], published: true },
  { code: "RCT101", title: "React", fee: 5999, tags: ["javascript"], published: false }
])

// Read
db.courses.find()                                          // all
db.courses.find({ published: true })                       // equality
db.courses.find({ fee: { $gt: 5000 } })                    // fee > 5000
db.courses.find({ tags: "java" })                          // array contains
db.courses.find({ $or: [{ fee: { $lt: 5000 } }, { tags: "spring" }] })
db.courses.find({}, { title: 1, fee: 1, _id: 0 })          // projection
db.courses.find().sort({ fee: -1 }).limit(2)               // top 2 by fee
db.courses.findOne({ code: "JAVA101" })
db.courses.countDocuments({ published: true })

// Update
db.courses.updateOne({ code: "RCT101" }, { $set: { published: true } })
db.courses.updateMany({ tags: "java" }, { $inc: { fee: 500 } })
db.courses.updateOne({ code: "JAVA101" }, { $push: { tags: "core" } })
db.courses.updateOne({ code: "NEW1" }, { $set: { title: "New" } }, { upsert: true })

// Delete
db.courses.deleteOne({ code: "NEW1" })
db.courses.deleteMany({ published: false })
```

Common operators: comparison `$eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin`; logical `$and $or $not`; element `$exists $type`; update `$set $unset $inc $push $pull $addToSet`.

## Aggregation
The **aggregation pipeline** processes documents through stages, similar to Java streams or SQL `GROUP BY`.

```javascript
db.enrollments.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "COMPLETED" } },                       // WHERE
  { $group: { _id: "$courseCode",                            // GROUP BY
              learners: { $sum: 1 },
              avgScore: { $avg: "$score" } } },
  { $sort: { learners: -1 } },                               // ORDER BY
  { $limit: 5 },                                             // LIMIT
  { $lookup: { from: "courses", localField: "_id",           // JOIN
               foreignField: "code", as: "course" } },
  { $project: { _id: 0, code: "$_id", learners: 1,
                avgScore: { $round: ["$avgScore", 1] },
                title: { $first: "$course.title" } } }
])
```

Other useful stages: `$unwind` (one document per array element), `$addFields`, `$count`, `$facet`, `$bucket`.

## Indexing
Without an index, MongoDB scans every document (a **COLLSCAN**).

```javascript
db.courses.createIndex({ code: 1 }, { unique: true })        // unique single-field
db.courses.createIndex({ published: 1, fee: -1 })            // compound
db.courses.createIndex({ title: "text" })                    // text search
db.sessions.createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 })  // TTL
db.courses.getIndexes()
db.courses.find({ published: true }).sort({ fee: -1 }).explain("executionStats")
```

Look for `IXSCAN` in the plan and compare `totalDocsExamined` to `nReturned`. Like SQL, compound indexes follow a prefix rule and every index costs write time and memory.

## Using MongoDB from Java
Spring Boot projects use **Spring Data MongoDB**: annotate a class with `@Document`, extend `MongoRepository<Course, String>`, and get CRUD methods plus derived queries such as `findByTagsContaining(String tag)`. Never build a filter from raw client JSON - accept specific, validated fields to avoid operator injection (for example a user sending `{"$ne": null}` as a password).

## Common mistakes
- Treating MongoDB as schemaless and storing inconsistent shapes.
- Embedding arrays that grow forever (16 MB document limit).
- Querying without indexes on large collections.
- Designing MongoDB collections like normalised SQL tables and then joining everything with `$lookup`.

## Practice exercise
1. Create a `training` database and a `courses` collection with schema validation.
2. Insert 8 courses with tags, an embedded trainer and embedded modules.
3. Query: published courses under 6000 sorted by fee; courses tagged "java"; titles only.
4. Add a `$push` of a new module and a `$inc` of fees for one tag.
5. Create an `enrollments` collection and write an aggregation for learners and average score per course.
6. Add indexes, run `explain("executionStats")` and confirm `IXSCAN`.

## Key takeaways
- NoSQL covers document, key-value, column-family and graph models.
- MongoDB stores BSON documents in collections; `_id` is the primary key.
- Embed bounded data read together; reference shared or unbounded data.
- Use `find`/`update`/`delete` operators for CRUD and pipelines for aggregation.
- Index according to your filters and sorts, and validate document shape.

Which aggregation stage is similar to SQL GROUP BY?

lessons.title: Gradle
lessons.description: Section 4 · Build Tools. Explain why build tools exist and set up Gradle with the wrapper.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Explain why build tools exist and set up Gradle with the wrapper.
- Configure build.gradle with plugins, repositories, dependencies and tasks.
- Use the build lifecycle, property-based build variants and multi-project builds.

## Introduction to Gradle
A real Java project has hundreds of source files and dozens of libraries. Compiling with `javac` by hand does not scale. A **build tool** automates compiling, downloading dependencies, running tests, packaging JARs and publishing artifacts - the same way on every machine and on the CI server.

**Gradle** is a modern build tool used by Spring Boot, Android and many enterprise projects. Builds are written in a **Groovy** (`build.gradle`) or **Kotlin** (`build.gradle.kts`) DSL. Its main alternative is **Maven** (XML `pom.xml`); both use the same Maven Central repository.

| | Gradle | Maven |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build script | Groovy/Kotlin DSL | XML |
| Flexibility | Very flexible, custom tasks are easy | Convention-driven, fixed lifecycle |
| Speed | Incremental builds, build cache, daemon | Generally slower on large builds |

## Installation and the Gradle Wrapper
Install Gradle (from gradle.org, SDKMAN `sdk install gradle`, or Homebrew), then check:

```bash
gradle --version
```

In practice you rarely use a global Gradle. Projects include the **Gradle Wrapper** - scripts that download and run the exact Gradle version the project expects:

```bash
gradle wrapper              # generate wrapper files once
./gradlew build             # macOS/Linux
gradlew.bat build           # Windows
```

Commit `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat` and the `gradle/wrapper/` folder so every developer and CI server uses the same version. Spring Initializr projects already include the wrapper.

Create a new project interactively with `gradle init` (choose application, Java, Groovy DSL, JUnit Jupiter).

### Standard project layout
```
my-app/
├── settings.gradle            # project name, included subprojects
├── build.gradle               # build logic for this project
├── gradlew, gradlew.bat, gradle/wrapper/
└── src/
    ├── main/java/             # application code
    ├── main/resources/        # config files (application.properties)
    ├── test/java/             # tests
    └── test/resources/
```

Build output goes to `build/` - add it to `.gitignore`.

## build.gradle explained
```groovy
plugins {
    id 'java'
    id 'application'
}

group = 'com.shimento'
version = '1.0.0'

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)   // Gradle provisions/uses JDK 21
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()                                     // where dependencies come from
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'com.google.guava:guava:33.2.1-jre'
    implementation 'com.mysql:mysql-connector-j:8.4.0'
    testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.3'
    testRuntimeOnly 'org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher'
}

application {
    mainClass = 'com.shimento.App'
}

test {
    useJUnitPlatform()                                 // run JUnit 5 tests
}
```

Reading it top to bottom: **plugins** add capabilities, `group`/`version` identify the artifact, the **toolchain** fixes the Java version, **repositories** say where to download libraries, **dependencies** list them, and the `application` and `test` blocks configure tasks. A misspelled block or property fails the build with an error naming the line - read Gradle's messages carefully.

## Dependencies
A dependency is written as `group:name:version` (its Maven coordinates). The **configuration** controls where it is visible:

| Configuration | Available at | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `implementation` | Compile + runtime of main code | Spring Web, Guava |
| `api` (`java-library` plugin) | Like implementation, but exposed to consumers of your library | Shared model types |
| `compileOnly` | Compile time only | Lombok annotations |
| `runtimeOnly` | Runtime only | JDBC driver |
| `annotationProcessor` | Compile-time processing | Lombok, MapStruct |
| `testImplementation` | Test compile + runtime | JUnit, Mockito |
| `testRuntimeOnly` | Test runtime only | JUnit platform launcher |

Gradle also downloads **transitive dependencies** (dependencies of your dependencies). Inspect them with:

```bash
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-databind
```

A **BOM (bill of materials)** aligns versions of related libraries: `implementation platform('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.3.4')`. The Spring Boot plugin manages these versions for you, so you can omit them.

## Plugins
**Plugins** add tasks and conventions.

```groovy
plugins {
    id 'java'                                              // compile, test, jar tasks
    id 'org.springframework.boot' version '3.3.4'          // bootRun, bootJar
    id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.6'   // version management
    id 'jacoco'                                            // test coverage reports
}
```

Core plugins (`java`, `application`, `java-library`, `jacoco`) need no version; community plugins come from the Gradle Plugin Portal and need one.

## Build lifecycle and tasks
Gradle runs a build in three phases:
1. **Initialization** - reads `settings.gradle` and decides which projects take part.
2. **Configuration** - evaluates every `build.gradle` and builds a graph of tasks.
3. **Execution** - runs the requested tasks and their dependencies in order.

Common tasks from the Java plugin:

```bash
./gradlew tasks           # list available tasks
./gradlew compileJava     # compile main code
./gradlew test            # run tests (report: build/reports/tests/test/index.html)
./gradlew jar             # package a JAR
./gradlew build           # compile + test + package (assemble + check)
./gradlew clean           # delete build/
./gradlew run             # run the application plugin's main class
./gradlew bootRun         # run a Spring Boot app
./gradlew build --scan    # detailed online build report
```

Tasks are **incremental**: if inputs have not changed, Gradle reports them as `UP-TO-DATE` and skips them. A custom task:

```groovy
tasks.register('hello') {
    group = 'custom'
    description = 'Prints a greeting'
    doLast { println "Building ${project.name} ${version}" }
}
```

## Build profiles
Gradle has no built-in "profiles" like Maven, but you can vary a build with **properties**:

```groovy
// build.gradle
def env = project.findProperty('env') ?: 'dev'

tasks.named('processResources') {
    filesMatching('application.properties') {
        expand(environment: env)
    }
}

if (env == 'prod') {
    tasks.named('test') { maxParallelForks = 4 }
}
```

```bash
./gradlew build -Penv=prod
```

Properties can also live in `gradle.properties` (project or user home). In Spring Boot, runtime environments are usually selected with **Spring profiles** (`spring.profiles.active=prod`, Module 28) rather than different builds - build one artifact and configure it per environment.

## Multi-project builds
Larger systems split code into modules that build together:

```
lms/
├── settings.gradle
├── build.gradle            # shared configuration
├── common/                 # shared DTOs and utilities
├── api/                    # Spring Boot REST service
└── worker/                 # background job service
```

```groovy
// settings.gradle
rootProject.name = 'lms'
include 'common', 'api', 'worker'

// build.gradle (root)
subprojects {
    apply plugin: 'java'
    repositories { mavenCentral() }
    java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }
}

// api/build.gradle
dependencies {
    implementation project(':common')        // depend on another module
}
```

```bash
./gradlew :api:test       # run one subproject's task
./gradlew build           # build everything in dependency order
```

## Common mistakes
- Using a different local Gradle instead of the committed wrapper.
- Hard-coding dependency versions that conflict with the Spring Boot BOM.
- Using `implementation` for a JDBC driver needed only at runtime (works, but `runtimeOnly` is clearer).
- Forgetting `useJUnitPlatform()`, so JUnit 5 tests do not run.
- Committing the `build/` folder.

## Practice exercise
1. Run `gradle init` to create a Java application with JUnit 5.
2. Configure a Java 21 toolchain, add Guava and a JUnit test, and run `./gradlew build`.
3. Add a custom task `printVersion` and run it.
4. Inspect transitive dependencies of one library.
5. Convert the project to a multi-project build with `common` and `app` subprojects where `app` uses a class from `common`.

## Key takeaways
- Gradle automates compile, test, package and dependency management.
- Always use the committed wrapper (`./gradlew`).
- `build.gradle` declares plugins, repositories, dependencies and task configuration.
- Configurations (`implementation`, `runtimeOnly`, `testImplementation`) control dependency visibility.
- Builds run in initialization, configuration and execution phases; multi-project builds share configuration.

lessons.title: Git
lessons.description: Section 5 · Version Control. Create repositories and record changes with staged, focused commits.
lessons.content:
## Learning objectives
- Create repositories and record changes with staged, focused commits.
- Work on branches and integrate them with merge or rebase, resolving conflicts.
- Use cherry-pick and stash to move specific changes and shelve work.

## Introduction to Git
**Git** is a distributed **version control system**. It records snapshots of your project over time so you can see who changed what and why, go back to any earlier version, work on features in parallel and merge everyone's work. Every developer has the full history locally, so most operations are fast and work offline.

Install Git from git-scm.com (Windows includes Git Bash), then set your identity once:

```bash
git --version
git config --global user.name "Asha Kumar"
git config --global user.email "asha@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

### The three areas
```
Working directory  --git add-->  Staging area (index)  --git commit-->  Repository (.git history)
```

- **Working directory** - the files you edit.
- **Staging area** - the changes you have selected for the next commit.
- **Repository** - the committed history stored in the hidden `.git` folder.

## Repository
A **repository (repo)** is a project folder tracked by Git.

```bash
mkdir training-portal && cd training-portal
git init                        # create a new repo
# or copy an existing remote repo:
git clone https://github.com/org/training-portal.git
```

Tell Git what to ignore with a `.gitignore` file in the root:

```
build/
node_modules/
.idea/
*.log
.env
```

Never commit build output, dependencies, IDE settings or secrets.

## Essential Git commands
| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `git status` | Show changed, staged and untracked files |
| `git add <file>` / `git add .` | Stage changes |
| `git commit -m "message"` | Record staged changes as a commit |
| `git log --oneline --graph` | Show history compactly |
| `git diff` / `git diff --staged` | Show unstaged / staged changes |
| `git restore <file>` | Discard working-directory changes to a file |
| `git restore --staged <file>` | Unstage a file |
| `git rm <file>` / `git mv a b` | Remove / rename a tracked file |
| `git remote -v` | List remote repositories |
| `git fetch` | Download remote history without changing your branch |
| `git pull` | Fetch and integrate remote changes into your branch |
| `git push` | Upload your commits to the remote |
| `git show <commit>` | Show one commit's changes |
| `git revert <commit>` | Create a new commit that undoes an earlier one (safe on shared branches) |
| `git reset` | Move the branch pointer (rewrites history - use carefully) |

## Commit
A **commit** is a snapshot with a unique hash, an author, a timestamp, a message and a pointer to its parent commit(s).

```bash
git add src/CourseService.java
git commit -m "Add course search by title"
```

Good commits are **small and focused** (one logical change) and have clear messages:

```
Add pagination to course list endpoint

Limit page size to 50 and sort by id as a tiebreaker so results are stable.
```

Write the subject in the imperative mood ("Add", "Fix", "Refactor"), under ~50 characters. Many teams use Conventional Commits: `feat: add course search`, `fix: handle empty title`.

`git commit --amend` changes the most recent commit (only before you have pushed it).

## Branch
A **branch** is a lightweight movable pointer to a commit. Branches let you develop features in isolation without breaking `main`.

```bash
git branch                          # list branches (* marks the current one)
git switch -c feature/course-search # create and switch
git switch main                     # switch back
git branch -d feature/course-search # delete a merged branch
git push -u origin feature/course-search   # publish and track
```

`HEAD` is a pointer to the branch (or commit) you currently have checked out. A typical team flow: create a branch per feature or fix from `main`, commit, push, open a pull request (Module 25), merge after review.

## Merge
**Merging** integrates another branch's changes into the current branch.

```bash
git switch main
git pull                            # make sure main is current
git merge feature/course-search
```

- **Fast-forward merge** - if `main` has no new commits, Git just moves the pointer forward.
- **Three-way merge** - if both branches have new commits, Git creates a **merge commit** with two parents.

### Merge conflicts
When both branches change the same lines, Git cannot decide and marks a conflict:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
int pageSize = 20;
=======
int pageSize = 50;
>>>>>>> feature/course-search
```

Resolve by editing the file to the correct final content (understanding both intentions), removing the markers, then:

```bash
git add CourseService.java
git commit                 # completes the merge
# or abandon: git merge --abort
```

Run the tests after resolving - a conflict-free merge can still be logically wrong.

## Rebase
**Rebasing** replays your branch's commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history.

```bash
git switch feature/course-search
git rebase main            # move my commits on top of the latest main
# if conflicts: fix, git add <file>, git rebase --continue   (or git rebase --abort)
```

```
Before:  main:    A---B---C
                       \
         feature:       D---E

After:   main:    A---B---C
                           \
         feature:           D'---E'
```

| Merge | Rebase |
| --- | --- |
| Preserves exact history with merge commits | Creates a clean, linear history |
| Safe for shared branches | Rewrites commits (new hashes) |
| Can produce a noisy graph | Easier to read and bisect |

**Golden rule:** never rebase commits that others have already pulled (shared/public branches). Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) can squash and reword your own local commits before sharing them.

## Cherry-pick
**Cherry-pick** applies the changes from one specific commit onto your current branch, creating a new commit.

```bash
git log --oneline main
# a1b2c3d Fix null pointer in enrollment
git switch release/1.2
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
```

Typical use: bringing a hotfix from `main` into a release branch without merging everything else. Overusing it duplicates commits across branches, so prefer merges for regular integration.

## Stash
**Stash** temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch context with a clean working directory.

```bash
git stash push -m "half-done search UI"    # save and clean the working directory
git switch main                            # fix an urgent bug...
git switch feature/course-search
git stash list                             # stash@{0}: On feature...: half-done search UI
git stash pop                              # reapply and remove from the stash
# git stash apply keeps it in the stash; git stash drop deletes it
```

Use `git stash -u` to include untracked files.

## Common mistakes
- Committing secrets (`.env`, passwords) - removing them from history is hard; rotate the secret immediately.
- Giant commits mixing unrelated changes.
- Working directly on `main` in a team.
- Rebasing or force-pushing a shared branch.
- Resolving conflicts by blindly choosing one side.

## Practice exercise
1. Initialise a repo for your Module 1 Java project with a proper `.gitignore`; make three focused commits.
2. Create `feature/average` and `feature/validation` branches that both edit the same method; merge one, then resolve the conflict when merging the other.
3. Create another branch and rebase it onto `main`; compare `git log --graph` with the merge result.
4. Cherry-pick a single bug-fix commit onto a `release` branch.
5. Stash an unfinished change, switch branches, then restore it with `git stash pop`.

## Key takeaways
- Git moves changes from working directory → staging area → repository.
- Make small, well-described commits and ignore generated files and secrets.
- Branches isolate work; merges integrate it; conflicts need human judgement and re-testing.
- Rebase gives linear history but never rebase shared commits.
- Cherry-pick copies individual commits; stash shelves unfinished work.
